For at that time agriculture was vigorously encouraged and wasteland was reclaimed; no land lay fallow, people devoted themselves to primary occupations; military colonies and the salt-exchange system were also established to supply border troops, so transport grain did not depend on county officials — hence both court and countryside had enough, and army and people alike were affluent.

外 contrasts with the household's place of origin here and does not mean a foreign country.

山西 and 真定 are parallel places whose people were moved to Fengyang; the current idiomatic text omits Shanxi.

At this time Deng Yu, Tang He, and other generals were dispatched to colonize Shaanxi, Zhangde, Runing, Beiping, and Yongping; people of Shanxi and Zhending were moved to colonize at Fengyang.

校舍 abbreviates the personnel categories 校尉 and 舍人 in Ming usage. It refers to imperial guards and hereditary military retainers, not school estates or guard residences.

At first, in Shizong's reign, the six estates and two lakes of Chengtian totaled 8,300-odd qing, supervised by eunuch officials; school estates were also permitted to merge and annex, increasing by 880 qing, divided into twelve estates.

At first, during Shizong's reign, the six estates and two lakes of Chengtian totaled more than 8,300 qing and were administered by eunuchs; imperial guards and hereditary military retainers were also allowed to annex land, adding 880 qing, and the holdings were divided into twelve estates.
The literal field should expand 校舍 as the personnel categories 校尉 and 舍人; the proposal's 'residences' still treats 舍 as a building.

For at that time agriculture was vigorously encouraged and wasteland was reclaimed; no land lay fallow, people devoted themselves to primary occupations; military colonies and the salt-exchange system were also established to supply border troops, so transport grain did not depend on county officials — hence both court and countryside had enough, and army and people alike were affluent.

For at that time agriculture was vigorously encouraged and wasteland reclaimed; no land lay fallow, and the people devoted themselves to their primary occupations. Military colonies and the salt-exchange system were also established to provision the frontier armies, so transport and supplies did not have to rely on the government. Thus both high and low had enough, and soldiers and civilians alike prospered.
縣官 denotes the government in this classical usage, not county officials; the revision also restores coherent English syntax.

The reason was that in those years the state pressed hard to encourage farming and open new land; fields were not left wild, and people held faithfully to their base occupations. Military colonies and the salt-exchange system were also set up to feed frontier armies, so supply convoys did not have to rely on county government — and thus both high and low had plenty, soldiers and civilians alike.

In those years the state vigorously promoted farming and opened new land. Fields did not lie fallow, and people kept to agriculture. Military colonies and the salt-exchange system provisioned the frontier armies without drawing transport and supplies from the government, so court and country had enough and soldiers and civilians alike prospered.
The idiomatic field repeats the mistaken county-government reading and benefits from a clearer causal sequence.
